
Header: `winui/ui/Animation.hpp`.

Which end of the curve the easing is applied to. EaseOut is the default.

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `EaseOut` | The curve is mirrored so it decelerates into the end; the default. |
| `EaseIn` | The curve as defined: accelerates out of the start. |

### KeyFrameKind

```cpp
enum class KeyFrameKind
```

Header: `winui/ui/Animation.hpp`.

How a key frame's segment gets from the previous value to its own.

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `Linear` | Interpolates linearly. |
| `Discrete` | Holds the previous value, then jumps at the key time. |
| `Spline` | Follows a cubic Bézier; the `easing` must be a [CubicBezier](../rendering/cubic-bezier.md). |
| `Easing` | Follows the `easing` curve. |

### AutomationRole

```cpp
enum class AutomationRole
```

Header: `winui/ui/Automation.hpp`.

What kind of thing a control is, as reported to accessibility clients such as screen readers. The default, `Group`, is right for every plain container. A `Group` node still appears in the accessibility tree, as a grouping node with no interaction.

A control reports its role by overriding [Element::automation_role()](element.md#automation_role), and what it lets a client do through the provider interfaces it lists in [Element::automation_providers()](element.md#automation_providers).

Example: 
```cpp
// A custom rating control exposed like a Slider to screen readers.
class Stars final : public ui::Element, private ui::RangeValueProvider
{
public:
    ui::AutomationRole automation_role() const override { return ui::AutomationRole::Slider; }

protected:
    void automation_providers(ui::AutomationProviders& out) override { out.range_value = this; }
    // measure_override()/render_override() omitted

private:
    double range_value() const override { return rating_; }
    double range_minimum() const override { return 0.0; }
    double range_maximum() const override { return 5.0; }
    double range_small_change() const override { return 1.0; }
    bool   range_read_only() const override { return false; }
    bool   set_range_value(double value) override { rating_ = value; return true; }

    double rating_ = 3.0;
};
```

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `Group` | Generic container with no more specific semantics ([StackControl](../layout/stack.md#uistackcontrol), [Grid](../layout/grid.md#uigrid), ...). |
| `Pane` | A scrollable/major content region ([Scroll](../layout/scroll.md#uiscroll), the window's own root). |
| `Button` | A push button. |
| `CheckBox` | A two- or three-state check box. |
| `RadioButton` | One option of a mutually exclusive group. |
| `Edit` | Single/multi-line text entry ([TextBox](../controls/text-box.md#uitextbox), [NumberBox](../controls/number-box.md#uinumberbox)'s edit part, ...). |
| `Text` | Static, read-only text ([TextControl](../controls/text.md#uitextcontrol)). |
| `Image` | A picture or icon ([Image](../controls/image.md#uiimage), [AnimatedIcon](../controls/animated-icon.md#uianimatedicon)). |
| `List` | A list of items. |
| `ListItem` | One entry of a List. |
| `ComboBox` | A drop-down selector ([ComboBox](../controls/combo-box.md#uicombobox)). |
| `Slider` | A control that sets a bounded value ([Slider](../controls/slider.md#uislider), [AnnotatedScrollBar](../layout/annotated-scroll-bar.md#uiannotatedscrollbar)). |
| `ProgressBar` | A progress indicator. |
| `Tab` | The tab strip/container ([Tabs](../controls/tabs.md#uitabs), [NavigationShell](../controls/navigation-shell.md#uinavigationshell), [SelectorBar](../controls/selector-bar.md#uiselectorbar)). |
| `TabItem` | One tab of a [Tab](../controls/tabs.md#uitab). |
| `Tree` | A hierarchical list ([TreeView](../controls/tree-view.md#uitreeview)). |
| `TreeItem` | One node of a Tree. |
| `Menu` | A popup menu of commands. |
| `MenuItem` | One command of a Menu or [MenuBar](../controls/menu-bar.md#uimenubar). |
| `MenuBar` | A horizontal bar of top-level menus. |
| `ToolBar` | A bar of commands. |
| `Hyperlink` | A navigation link. |
| `Document` | A rich, multi-paragraph text surface. |
| `Header` | A row of column headers. |
| `HeaderItem` | One column header of a Header. |
| `Separator` | A visual divider with no interaction ([AppBarSeparator](../controls/app-bar-button.md#uiappbarseparator)). |
| `SpinButton` | An up/down value stepper. |
| `Thumb` | A draggable divider/handle with no bounded value ([Splitter](../layout/splitter.md#uisplitter)); [Slider](../controls/slider.md#uislider) has one. |
| `SplitButton` | A button with a second part that opens a flyout ([SplitButton](../controls/split-button.md#uisplitbutton), [ToggleSplitButton](../controls/split-button.md#uitogglesplitbutton)). |
| `DataGrid` | A table of rows and columns ([TableView](../controls/table-view.md#uitableview)). |
| `DataItem` | One row of a data grid ([TableView](../controls/table-view.md#uitableview)). |
| `Custom` | Something with real semantics that doesn't map to any role above. |
| `TitleBar` | A window's caption with its buttons, when the theme draws it (Frame::Themed). |
| `Calendar` | A month calendar ([CalendarView](../controls/calendar-view.md#uicalendarview)): a grid of days with Selection and [Grid](../layout/grid.md#uigrid) patterns. |

### Alignment

```cpp
enum class Alignment
```

Header: `winui/ui/Element.hpp`.

How an element is placed within the (possibly larger) rect its parent affords it on one axis, once margin/min-size are accounted for. [`Stretch`](../rendering/namespace-ui.md#stretch), the default, hands the element the whole rect. The other three shrink the element to its own desired extent and position it within the rect. A stack's `child_alignment` uses the same values for all of its children at once, on the axis across the stack (see Stack.hpp).

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `Leading` | left / top |
| `Center` | centered in the slot |
| `Trailing` | right / bottom |
| `Stretch` | fills the slot, up to the max size (the default) |

### HitRegion

```cpp
enum class HitRegion
```

Header: `winui/ui/Element.hpp`.

What a press at a point means to the window around it, for a window whose content stands in for its caption: a `Frame::Borderless` window, or content extended into the title bar. Resize edges depend on DPI frame metrics, so the host classifies those itself before asking the tree. The caption-button values are for a caption the app draws itself: the press still reaches the element under it, and the host tells the OS what is there.

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `Client` | an ordinary click, delivered to the element |
| `Caption` | the window's caption: drag to move, double-click to maximize, right-click for the system menu |
| `SystemMenu` | The window icon in a drawn caption: a click opens the system menu, a double-click closes the window. Handled by the OS, not delivered to the element. |
| `MinimizeButton` | A drawn caption's minimize button. A client click, delivered to the element. |
| `MaximizeButton` | A drawn caption's maximize or restore button. Delivered to the element like a client click. Where the system offers snap layouts, hovering it also opens their flyout. |
| `CloseButton` | A drawn caption's close button. A client click, delivered to the element. |

### WindowState

```cpp
enum class WindowState
```

Header: `winui/ui/WindowShell.hpp`.

The state a window is in, read through [Window::state()](window.md#state) and asked for with [Window::request_state()](window.md#request_state). Two things are not states:

- A snapped or arranged window (snap layouts, Win+Left/Right) is in the Normal state. The OS controls snapping, and an app cannot request it.
- Exclusive fullscreen, where the app owns the display mode, is not supported. `Fullscreen` is the borderless kind that browsers and video players use.

[Visibility](#visibility) ([Window::visible()](window.md#visible)) and always-on-top ([WindowStyle::always_on_top](window-style.md)) are independent of the state.

Example: 
```cpp
window.set_content(ui::Button{
    .text = ui::bind(window.state(), [](ui::WindowState s) {
        return std::string{s == ui::WindowState::Maximized ? "Restore" : "Maximize"}; }),
    .on_click = [&] {
        if (window.state().get() == ui::WindowState::Maximized) window.restore();
        else window.request_state(ui::WindowState::Maximized);
    },
});
```

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `Normal` | framed, at its normal bounds (possibly snapped) |
| `Minimized` | a taskbar button only |
| `Maximized` | fills the monitor's work area; the taskbar stays visible |
| `Fullscreen` | covers the whole monitor, with no caption or border |

### Frame

```cpp
enum class Frame
```

Header: `winui/ui/WindowStyle.hpp`.

How much of the frame the OS draws ([WindowStyle::frame](window-style.md)).

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `Standard` | The OS caption and border. The default. |
| `Borderless` | No caption and no visible border. The system still treats it as a normal window, so snap layouts, Win+arrow keys, shake to minimize, the minimize animation, the drop shadow and Alt+Space's system menu keep working. Resize edges follow `resizable`. Dragging needs a region that answers HitRegion::Caption ([TitleBar](../controls/title-bar.md#uititlebar), [DragArea](../controls/drag-area.md#uidragarea)). |
| `None` | A bare popup: no caption, no border, no resizing, no shadow and no snapping. For splash screens and overlays. WindowState::Fullscreen uses this frame too. |
| `Themed` | The theme draws the caption and the border in its era's style. Underneath it is `Borderless`, so snapping, Win+arrow keys, the system menu and the drop shadow keep working, and hovering the drawn maximize button opens the snap layouts where the system has them. Corners are square. The caption shows the window's icon, and screen readers see it as a title bar with its three buttons. A theme with no frame of its own (Fluent 2, Fluent, MDL2) gives `Standard`, and switching themes switches between the two live. |

### Backdrop

```cpp
enum class Backdrop
```

Header: `winui/ui/WindowStyle.hpp`.

The system material behind the window. Where the system has no backdrop materials, the window keeps its opaque background.

The theme can decline it ([ChromeHints::allows_system_backdrop](../themes/chrome-hints.md) does for every era before Windows 11, and for high contrast), and so can the system, for example with transparency effects off or in energy saver mode. Seeded by [`ui::WindowOptions::backdrop`](window-options.md), applied live through [Window::set_backdrop()](window.md#set_backdrop). While a backdrop is on, the client area is left transparent and [Window::background()](window.md#background) is not painted.

Example: 
```cpp
int main()
{
    ui::Window window{{.title = "Mica", .backdrop = ui::Backdrop::Mica}};
    window.set_content(ui::Button{
        .text     = "Switch to Acrylic",
        .on_click = [&window] { window.set_backdrop(ui::Backdrop::Acrylic); }, // applied live
    });
    return ui::run(window);
}
```

| Value | |
| --- | --- |
| `None` | No material: the window's opaque background. The default. |
| `Mica` | The desktop wallpaper, sampled once, tinting a long-lived window. |
| `MicaAlt` | Like Mica with a stronger tint, for tabbed windows. |
| `Acrylic` | A blurred, semi-transparent view of what is behind the window, updated continuously. |

## Functions

### animations_enabled

```cpp
bool animations_enabled()
```

Header: `winui/ui/Animation.hpp`.

Whether animations play right now. False while a [Window](window.md) whose theme has [Theme::animations_enabled](../themes/theme.md#animations_enabled) off is ticking, laying out, rendering or dispatching input to its tree. True outside any window. A control that runs its own tween checks it, or advances its clock by [animation_delta()](#animation_delta), so the tween jumps to its end state instead of playing.

Example: 
```cpp
class Drawer : public ui::Element
{
    static constexpr ui::Duration SlideTime = 250ms;
    ui::Duration                  slide_{};

    void tick_override(ui::Duration delta) override
    {
        slide_ = std::min(slide_ + ui::animation_delta(delta), SlideTime);
        mark_dirty(ui::DirtyFlags::Visual);
    }
};
```

### animation_delta

```cpp
Duration animation_delta(Duration delta)
```

Header: `winui/ui/Animation.hpp`.

How far an animation's clock moves in a tick of `delta`: `delta` itself, or, while [animations_enabled()](#animations_enabled) is false, far enough to finish any finite animation in that one tick. Use it only for animations. A delay, a timeout, a blink or a looping indicator keeps counting `delta`.


Header: `winui/ui/Animation.hpp`.

The eased progress for linear progress `t` (0..1), with the curve applied at the end its [EasingMode](#easingmode) names. The curves may overshoot 0..1 (Back, Elastic).

The value of `frames` (sorted by time) at `time`. Each frame's segment starts at the previous frame's value, the first one's at `base` (the value the property had when the animation started). After the last frame its value holds.

### run

```cpp
int run(Window& window)
```

Header: `winui/ui/App.hpp`.

Show `window` and run the message loop until it is closed; returns the exit code.

The window is the app's main window. It is created from its [WindowOptions](window-options.md) if it has no OS window yet, and the loop also runs every other window the app shows ([Window::show()](window.md#show)) while it is open. Closing the main window ends the loop and closes whatever else is still open. [run()](#run) only borrows the window: it is an object the app owns, usually a local in `main()`, and it is still a valid, closed [Window](window.md) when [run()](#run) returns. Not re-entrant: one [run()](#run) at a time.

Returns -1 when the window could not be created, or on a platform with no backend.

Example: 
```cpp
int main()
{
    ui::Window window{{.title = "Demo", .size = {400, 300}}};
    ui::Property<int> clicks{0};
    window.set_content(ui::Button{.text = "Click", .on_click = [&] { ++clicks; }});
    return ui::run(window);
}
```

### run

```cpp
int run()
```

Header: `winui/ui/App.hpp`.

Run the message loop with no main window. Every window the app shows runs on it. Closing the last one does not end the loop, only [quit()](#quit) does. Returns [quit()](#quit)'s exit code, and closes whatever is still open on the way out. For apps whose entry point is not a window, such as a tray icon. Not re-entrant.

Example: 
```cpp
int main()
{
    ui::Window tool{{.title = "Tool", .size = {300, 200}}};
    tool.set_content(ui::Button{.text = "Quit", .on_click = [] { ui::quit(); }});
    tool.show();
    return ui::run(); // closing the window does not end the loop, quit() does
}
```

### open_window

```cpp
Window& open_window(std::unique_ptr<Window> window)
```

Header: `winui/ui/App.hpp`.

Shows `window` and hands it to the message loop, which destroys it between two messages once it has closed. To get rid of it, call `window.close()` from anywhere, its own handlers included. For an app's secondary windows, such as a tool window, an inspector or a document, that should go away when closed.

Returns the window, so you can set it up further. To reach it later, keep `window.ref()`. Its get() returns null once the window is gone, and its is_open() tells bound UI when it closes. UI thread only.

Example: 
```cpp
auto about = std::make_unique<ui::Window>(ui::WindowOptions{.title = "About", .size = {320, 200}});
ui::Window& w = *about;
about->set_content(ui::Button{.text = "Close", .on_click = [&w] { w.close(); }});
ui::open_window(std::move(about));
```

### quit

```cpp
void quit(int exit_code = 0)
```

Header: `winui/ui/App.hpp`.

End the running loop (either [run()](#run)) with `exit_code`. Posted, so the handler calling it returns first. UI thread only.

### automation_children

```cpp
std::vector<Element*> automation_children(const Element& node)
```

Header: `winui/ui/AutomationTree.hpp`.

The children an accessibility client sees under `node`, in navigation order.

A decorative node ([Accessibility::decorative](accessibility.md#decorative)) or a [NativeControl](../controls/native-control.md#uinativecontrol) (automation_is_native_host()) is skipped, and its own children appear in its place as children of `node`. A collapsed node (Visibility::Collapsed) is left out with everything in it, since none of it is on screen. While `node` has a popup open, the popup's content comes last, unless that content names a closer parent through automation_parent_of(), as a submenu does with its item.

The returned pointers are non-owning and valid until the tree changes. Each call walks the tree again.

Example: 
```cpp
// The row only lays the buttons out, so it is marked decorative.
window.set_content(ui::VerticalStack{
    .content = {
        ui::Text{.text = "Unsaved changes"},
        ui::HorizontalStack{
            .accessibility = {.decorative = true},
            .content       = {ui::Button{.text = "Save"}, ui::Button{.text = "Discard"}},
        },
    },
});

// What a screen reader finds under the form: the text and both buttons, the row spliced out.
for (ui::Element* child : ui::automation_children(*window.content()))
{
    std::println("{}", child->automation_name()); // Unsaved changes, Save, Discard
}
```

### automation_providers

```cpp
AutomationProviders automation_providers(const Element& node)
```

Header: `winui/ui/AutomationTree.hpp`.

What an accessibility client can do with `node`: the provider for each pattern it supports now, null for the others ([Element::automation_providers()](element.md#automation_providers)). Screen readers reach a control through these, and a test can drive one the same way.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::CheckBoxControl check_box{"Remember me"};
if (ui::ToggleProvider* toggle = ui::automation_providers(check_box).toggle)
{
    toggle->toggle_next(); // as a screen reader's Toggle does
}
```

### automation_parent

```cpp
Element* automation_parent(const Element& node)
```

Header: `winui/ui/AutomationTree.hpp`.

The nearest ancestor that [automation_children()](#automation_children) would not skip, or nullptr at the root. It is the inverse of [automation_children()](#automation_children): `automation_parent(*child)` is the node whose [automation_children()](#automation_children) lists `child`.

Example: 
```cpp
// Continuing the automation_children() example: with Save or Discard focused, the node above
// it is the form, because the decorative row between them is skipped.
if (ui::Element* focused = window.focused())
{
    ui::Element* group = ui::automation_parent(*focused); // window.content()
}
```

### automation_focus

```cpp
Element* automation_focus(Element* focused)
```

Header: `winui/ui/AutomationTree.hpp`.

The node a client sees as focused while `focused` has keyboard focus. That is the item the control names inside itself through [Element::automation_focus()](element.md#automation_focus), followed as far as it goes (for a menu bar, the item in its open menu), or else `focused` itself. Returns nullptr for nullptr.

### automation_role_name

```cpp
const char* automation_role_name(AutomationRole role)
```

Header: `winui/ui/AutomationTree.hpp`.

A role's name as [describe_automation()](#describe_automation) prints it: "Button", "TreeItem".

### automation_value

```cpp
AutomationValue automation_value(const Element& node, AutomationProperty property)
```

Header: `winui/ui/AutomationTree.hpp`.

The value of `property` on `node` now.

### describe_automation

```cpp
std::string describe_automation(const Element& root)
```

Header: `winui/ui/AutomationTree.hpp`.

A text dump of the accessibility tree rooted at `root`, the same on every machine and resolution. It has one line for `root` and one for each node [automation_children()](#automation_children) reports below it, indented two spaces per level. A line holds the role, the quoted name if it is not empty, `#` and the [Accessibility::automation_id](accessibility.md#automation_id) if one is set, and a bracketed list of the supported patterns if there are any. Every line ends in `\n`.

It does for accessibility what [describe()](../rendering/namespace-ui.md#describe) does for rendering, and makes a stable check of what a screen reader sees in a test, with no window or accessibility client needed.

Example: 
```cpp
// Print what a screen reader sees of a window, e.g. while giving a custom control its role.
window.set_content(ui::VerticalStack{
    .content = {
        ui::Button{.text = "Save"},
        ui::CheckBox{.text = "Remember me"},
    },
});
std::print("{}", ui::describe_automation(*window.content()));
// Group
//   Button "Save" [Invoke]
//   CheckBox "Remember me" [Toggle=Off]
```

### clipboard

```cpp
Clipboard& clipboard()
```

Header: `winui/ui/Clipboard.hpp`.

The system clipboard, one for the whole process. It works from the first call, before any window exists. On a platform with no clipboard, it is an in-memory one. Use it on the UI thread.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::Property<std::string> report{"All tests passed"};
ui::ButtonControl         copy_button{"Copy report"};
copy_button.on_click([&] { ui::clipboard().set_text(report.get()); });
```

### standard_command

```cpp
Command standard_command(StandardCommand kind, CommandHandler execute = {}, Binding<bool> enabled = true)
```

Header: `winui/ui/Command.hpp`.

A [Command](command.md) with the standard text, symbol, shortcut and description of `kind`, running `execute` while `enabled`. Delete is "Delete", Symbol::Delete, the Delete key and "Delete the
selected content". The text and description come from [strings()](../core/namespace-ui.md#strings).commands and follow [set_strings()](../core/namespace-ui.md#set_strings). Any field set afterwards, before a control uses the command, wins.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::Property<bool> has_selection{false};
// Text "Delete", Symbol::Delete, the Delete key and the description come with the kind;
// the app adds what deleting means and when it is possible.
const ui::Command del = ui::standard_command(ui::StandardCommand::Delete,
                                             [&](std::string_view item) { remove_item(item); },
                                             has_selection);

// The button's text, icon, tooltip, shortcut and enabled state all come from `del`:
window.set_content(ui::CommandBar{
    .primary = {ui::AppBarButton{.command = del, .command_parameter = "List item 3"}},
});
```

### on_ui_thread

```cpp
UiThreadHop on_ui_thread(WindowRef window) noexcept
```

Header: `winui/ui/Coroutine.hpp`.

`co_await ui::on_ui_thread(home)` resumes the coroutine on the UI thread of the [Window](window.md) that `home` was taken from. Take `home` with [Window::ref()](window.md#ref) on the UI thread, before the work starts. The resumption goes through [Window::post()](window.md#post), so it runs inside the next tick(), ahead of on_tick(). It never resumes at once, even when the coroutine is already on the UI thread. Callable from any thread, also after the [Window](window.md) was destroyed, and it never reaches a new [Window](window.md) built at the old one's address.

When the window is closed or destroyed before that tick, the work is dropped and the coroutine never resumes. Its frame is destroyed instead, which runs the destructors of its locals, so nothing leaks. The frame is destroyed on the thread that dropped the work:
- the awaiting thread, when the window was already closed or destroyed
- the UI thread, when the window closes while the work is queued
- the destroying thread, when the [Window](window.md) is destroyed while the work is queued

A coroutine that has to clean up after itself does it in a destructor, such as an RAII guard, since code after the co_await may never run. Anything that awaits this coroutine in turn never resumes either.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::FireAndForget refresh(ui::Window& window, ui::Property<std::string>& status)
{
    const ui::WindowRef home = window.ref(); // still on the UI thread
    co_await ui::on_background();
    std::string text = fetch_status();
    co_await ui::on_ui_thread(home);
    status = std::move(text); // the property's observers run on the UI thread
}
```

### background_scheduler

```cpp
Scheduler& background_scheduler()
```

Header: `winui/ui/Coroutine.hpp`.

The [Scheduler](../core/scheduler.md) [on_background()](#on_background) uses when given none. It has one worker per hardware thread, is created on first use and is never destroyed. Its workers end with the process, so a coroutine waiting on it at exit is not resumed. A coroutine that hops back to a destroyed [Window](window.md) is dropped (see [on_ui_thread()](#on_ui_thread)).

### on_background

```cpp
BackgroundHop on_background(Scheduler& scheduler) noexcept
```

Header: `winui/ui/Coroutine.hpp`.

`co_await ui::on_background(scheduler)` resumes the coroutine on one of `scheduler`'s workers. Code running there must not touch the UI tree. In [Scheduler::Inline](../core/scheduler.md#struct-inline) mode it resumes at once on the calling thread. Every job queued on a [Scheduler](../core/scheduler.md) runs, also when the scheduler is destroyed, so a coroutine waiting here is always resumed.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::Scheduler pool{2};
auto work = [&]() -> ui::FireAndForget {
    co_await ui::on_background(pool);
    crunch();
};
work();
```

### on_background

```cpp
BackgroundHop on_background()
```

Header: `winui/ui/Coroutine.hpp`.

[`co_await ui::on_background()`](#on_background) resumes the coroutine on a worker of [background_scheduler()](#background_scheduler). It is meant for work that keeps a CPU busy. A long blocking wait, such as on a socket or a sleep, holds a worker the whole time, so give that its own [Scheduler](../core/scheduler.md) or thread.

The default pool is never joined, so work can still run on it after main() returned and the [Window](window.md) it hops back to is gone. [on_ui_thread()](#on_ui_thread) then drops the coroutine. Anything else the coroutine refers to has to outlive it, or must not be touched after that hop.

### set_jump_list

```cpp
void set_jump_list(std::vector<JumpTask> tasks)
```

Header: `winui/ui/JumpList.hpp`.

Sets the app's jump list, the menu the system shows on a right-click on the app's taskbar button or its entry in Start. `tasks` go in its Tasks section, in this order, above the Recent section that [ui::add_recent_file()](#add_recent_file) fills. An empty list removes the tasks.

A task starts the app again. That second start usually hands its arguments to the instance already running through [ui::claim_single_instance()](#claim_single_instance) and exits. The system stores the list, and it stays after the app quits until the next call replaces it. The list belongs to the app's taskbar button. When the app has set its own app identity, it is that identity's list, which the app's notifications also use. Otherwise it is the executable's. A system without jump lists ignores the call.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::set_jump_list({
    ui::JumpTask{.title = "New window", .arguments = "--new-window"},
    ui::JumpTask{.title = "New note", .arguments = "--new-note", .description = "Opens an empty note"},
});
```

### add_recent_file

```cpp
void add_recent_file(const std::filesystem::path& path)
```

Header: `winui/ui/JumpList.hpp`.

Records that the app opened the file at `path`, for the Recent section of its jump list and the system's list of recent files. The jump list shows it only for a file type the app is registered to open. Fire and forget. A system without the list ignores it.

Example: 
```cpp
if (const std::optional<std::filesystem::path> file = ui::pick_file(window))
{
    open_document(*file);
    ui::add_recent_file(*file);
}
```

### launch_uri

```cpp
void launch_uri(const std::string& uri)
```

Header: `winui/ui/Launcher.hpp`.

Opens `uri` with whatever app the OS has registered for it, fire and forget. An empty URI, or one nothing handles, does nothing.

Example: 
```cpp
window.set_content(ui::Button{.text = "Help", .on_click = [] { ui::launch_uri("https://example.com/help"); }});
ui::launch_uri("mailto:support@example.com"); // opens the mail client
```

### launch_file

```cpp
void launch_file(const std::filesystem::path& file)
```

Header: `winui/ui/Launcher.hpp`.

Opens `file` with the app registered for its type, as a double-click in the file manager does, fire and forget. An empty path, or one that does not exist, does nothing.

Example: 
```cpp
if (auto path = ui::pick_save_file(window, {.suggested_name = "report.pdf"}))
{
    save_document(*path);
    ui::launch_file(*path); // shows it in the PDF viewer
}
```

### message_box

```cpp
MessageBoxResult message_box(const Window& owner, const MessageBoxOptions& options)
```

Header: `winui/ui/MessageBox.hpp`.

Shows the operating system's own message box over `owner` and waits until the user answers. The owner is disabled meanwhile, and the app's other windows keep painting. The OS draws the box in its own style, whatever theme the app uses. For a box in the app's theme, use a [ui::Dialog](../controls/dialog.md#uidialog).

Example: 
```cpp
const ui::MessageBoxResult answer = ui::message_box(window,
    {.title   = "Notes",
     .heading = "Save changes to todo.txt?",
     .text    = "Your changes are lost if you don't save them.",
     .buttons = ui::MessageBoxButtons::YesNoCancel,
     .icon    = ui::MessageBoxIcon::Warning});
if (answer == ui::MessageBoxResult::Yes)
{
    save();
}
```

### message_box

```cpp
MessageBoxResult message_box(const MessageBoxOptions& options)
```

Header: `winui/ui/MessageBox.hpp`.

[ui::message_box()](#message_box) without an owner window, for a message before any window exists (a failed start-up) or after the last one closed. The box gets a taskbar button of its own.

Example: 
```cpp
int start(bool config_loaded)
{
    if (!config_loaded)
    {
        ui::message_box({.title = "Notes",
                         .text  = "The settings file is damaged.",
                         .icon  = ui::MessageBoxIcon::Error});
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### notify

```cpp
void notify(Notification notification)
```

Header: `winui/ui/Notification.hpp`.

Shows a desktop notification, a toast in the corner of the screen that also goes to the notification center. The app needs no tray icon and no installer. The first call registers the program with the system under its own name, so the toast shows the executable's description (or its file name) and its icon. The user's notification settings decide whether it shows, and do-not-disturb holds it back. Fire and forget. A system without notifications shows nothing.

A click reaches `on_click` while the app runs. Once the app has quit, clicking the entry in the notification center only removes it.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::notify({.title    = "Export finished",
            .text     = "report.pdf was saved to Documents.",
            .on_click = [&] { window.activate(); }});
```

### pick_file

```cpp
std::optional<std::filesystem::path> pick_file(const Window& owner, const PickFileOptions& options = {})
```

Header: `winui/ui/Pickers.hpp`.

The system's "open file" dialog, modal to `owner`. Returns the chosen file, or nothing if the user canceled. Blocks until the dialog closes; the window keeps painting meanwhile. Throws std::invalid_argument for a malformed extension, index or folder.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::Property<std::string> file_name;
window.set_content(ui::Button{.text = "Open...", .on_click = [&] {
    if (auto path = ui::pick_file(window, {.title      = "Pick an image",
                                           .file_types = {{.name = "Images", .extensions = {".png", ".jpg"}}}}))
    {
        file_name = ui::path_to_utf8(path->filename());
    }
}});
```

As [pick_file()](#pick_file), letting the user choose several files. Empty if the user canceled.


Header: `winui/ui/Printing.hpp`.

Shows the system print dialog over `owner`, where the user picks the printer, pages, copies and paper and sees a live preview of the pages. The app's windows keep handling input and painting meanwhile.

### draw_element

```cpp
void draw_element(Renderer& renderer, Element& content, const Rect& area, const PrintContext& context)
```

Header: `winui/ui/Printing.hpp`.

Lays [`content`](spec-vocabulary.md#content) out in `area` and draws it: a draw_page that prints controls or a built spec.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::print(window, ui::PrintJob{
    .title      = "Hello",
    .page_count = [](const ui::PrintPage&, const ui::PrintContext&) { return std::size_t{1}; },
    .draw_page  = [](ui::Renderer& renderer, const ui::PrintPage& page, const ui::PrintContext& context)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<ui::Element> sheet = ui::build(ui::Text{.text = "Hello", .role = ui::TextRole::Title});

});
```

### claim_single_instance

```cpp
bool claim_single_instance(std::string_view id, Callback<void(InstanceActivation)> on_activated)
```

Header: `winui/ui/SingleInstance.hpp`.

Makes this process the one instance of the program named `id` for the user's session.

The first process to claim `id` gets true and keeps the claim until it exits. A later start that claims the same `id` hands its command line to the first, which receives it through `on_activated` on its UI thread, and gets false: it should exit without opening a window. The running instance is allowed to bring its window to the front from `on_activated`.

`id` names the program, not the executable: pick something unique to the app, such as "com.example.notes". Call it from the UI thread, before the first window opens. A process that already holds the claim gets true again.

Example: 
```cpp
int main()
{
    ui::Window window{{.title = "Notes"}};
    if (!ui::claim_single_instance("com.example.notes",
                                   [&window](ui::InstanceActivation started)
                                   {
                                       if (started.arguments.size() > 1)
                                       {
                                           open_document(started.working_directory /
                                                         ui::path_from_utf8(started.arguments[1]));
                                       }
                                       window.activate();
                                   }))
    {
        return 0; // the running Notes opens the file
    }
    return ui::run(window);
}
```

### tray_flyout_options

```cpp
WindowOptions tray_flyout_options(TrayFlyoutOptions options = {})
```

Header: `winui/ui/TrayIcon.hpp`.

The [WindowOptions](window-options.md) of a tray flyout: a bare, always-on-top popup with rounded corners and no taskbar button, created hidden, that hides instead of closing. Construct an ordinary [Window](window.md) with it and hand that window to [TrayIconOptions::flyout](tray-icon-options.md).

Example: 
```cpp
ui::Window flyout{ui::tray_flyout_options({.title = "Timer", .width = 320.0f})};
```

### place_tray_flyout

```cpp
Point place_tray_flyout(const Rect& anchor, const Rect& work_area, Size size, float margin)
```

Header: `winui/ui/TrayIcon.hpp`.

Where a flyout of `size` goes, beside a tray icon at `anchor` on a monitor whose work area is `work_area`, in any unit as long as all four agree. Returns the top-left. The taskbar is on the edge of the work area that the anchor lies outside of. The flyout sits `margin` inside that edge, centered on the anchor along it and kept `margin` clear of the corners. An anchor inside the work area, such as one in the overflow flyout or an empty rect, is treated as a bottom taskbar.

Public for an app that places a window of its own the same way.

Example: 
```cpp
// A notes window of the app's own, opened beside the tray icon the way a flyout is. `icon` is
// the icon's rect in screen DIPs, wherever the app got it from.
ui::Window     notes{{.title = "Notes"}};
const ui::Rect icon{1000.0f, 1040.0f, 32.0f, 32.0f};
const ui::Size size{360.0f, 400.0f};
if (const std::optional<ui::Rect> work = notes.work_area())
{
    notes.resize(size);
    notes.move(ui::place_tray_flyout(icon, *work, size, 12.0f));
}
// With the icon at {1000, 1040, 32, 32} and a 1920x1032 work area above a bottom taskbar, the
// window goes to {836, 620}: centered on the icon, 12 DIPs above the taskbar.
```

### to_layout_paragraphs

```cpp
std::vector<TextLayoutParagraph> to_layout_paragraphs(const std::vector<Paragraph>& paragraphs, const TextStyle& base, int character_spacing, std::vector<const Inline*>* links = nullptr)
```

Header: `winui/ui/text/Inlines.hpp`.

Turns `paragraphs` into the runs a [TextLayout](../rendering/text-layout.md) lays out, with `base` as the block's style. Each run gets its inline's own formatting over `base`, and `character_spacing`. Links are underlined and tagged with their index in document order. When `links` is given, it receives the links in that order. Its pointers point into `paragraphs` and stay valid only as long as it does.
